Reviewer #3:

Bakkour and colleagues have done a quite good job addressing most of the reviewers' points, in particular the concerns about the multiple-comparison correction, the lesion information of patients, the analysis of chosen value signals, and the PPI analysis.

However, there are still some issues with the revised manuscript, so that we do not think that it can already be accepted in its current state.

1) In their rebuttal, the authors state that they compared their DDM version to simpler versions without power transformation and without a collapsing bound and found that (at least on the group level) their DDM version wins this comparison. However, none of this is reported in the manuscript, and we are wondering why. We strongly suggest that these comparisons should be reported, in particular, because the more conceptual justifications that are given are not convincing (e.g., the authors say "there is no reason to assume that the relationship [between value and drift] is linear"; speaking with Occam's Razor, we'd say "there is no reason NOT to assume a linear relationship"). Furthermore, the authors do not report a parameter recovery analysis that was asked for in the previous essential revisions.

2) The authors added a comparison of the DDM with a heuristic model. In general, we appreciate this interesting comparison. However, there are two issues that we have with this comparison.

First, for the heuristic model the authors draw RTs from a normal distribution. The authors may consider verifying whether the RTs in their task were indeed normally distributed. This may be the case given the 3 sec time limit, but often RTs are skewed. In that case, the authors may consider more appropriate distributions such as log-normal or ex-Gaussian to make the model comparison fair.

Second, the authors appear to struggle with the quantitative comparison between the two models, because they do not have a good error model for what they call "trivial" decisions. There is a simple (and very common) solution to this problem. Instead of punishing errors in "trivial" decisions by assuming a probability of p =.01, one would treat this probability p as a free parameter (i.e., assuming a so-called "trembling hand" error rate of p in trivial decisions). This "trembling hand" error is very common in research on strategy selection (e.g., Rieskamp and Otto, 2006, JEP General). Allowed values for p might be restricted to some plausible range (e.g., p <.1). This would render calling the comparison an "unsatisfactory exercise" unnecessary. Note, however, that we still think that the (also very interesting) qualitative comparison should remain in the paper, too.

3) Looking at the new ROI analyses reported in Figure 3—figure supplement 3E-H (and the associated Table 3—source data 8), we saw that there is actually hippocampal activity related to RT in the perceptual task. We think that this requires rephrasing the Abstract, in which it is stated that this relationship would be "not observed in a perceptual decision task". Instead, the significantly stronger relationship in value-based compared to perceptual decision making should be emphasized.

results.result: The study included 30 healthy young participants in Experiment 1 (fMRI) and 6 amnesic patients with 14 age-matched controls in Experiment 2. Patients had severe memory impairments but intact working memory and verbal IQ, with lesions primarily affecting the hippocampus and surrounding MTL.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C89-C94 provide comprehensive demographic, neuropsychological, and lesion characterization data for both experiments. The sample characteristics are clearly documented with appropriate detail including age, gender, neuropsychological test scores, and lesion extent. Ethical approvals are documented (C89-C90).

results.result: In healthy participants, decision time was longer when choice options were closer in value for both perceptual and value-based tasks. Choices and reaction times in both tasks were well described by drift diffusion models, with comparable choice functions and RT ranges across tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 and C26-C27 present behavioral findings with model fits shown in Figure 2. The drift diffusion model provided better fits than simpler alternatives (C27), and the behavioral patterns were comparable across tasks (C26), supporting the use of this modeling framework.

results.result: Hippocampal BOLD activity was more positively correlated with reaction time for value-based decisions than perceptual decisions. This effect was localized to hippocampal regions showing memory retrieval activity, as demonstrated by conjunction analysis, and remained significant after controlling for multiple potential confounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6 and C33-C35 present converging fMRI evidence from multiple analyses (main analysis, conjunction with memory localizer, control analyses accounting for difficulty and other factors). The hippocampal finding is robust across different analytical approaches and independent validation using meta-analysis maps (C35).

results.result: Functional connectivity between the hippocampus and parietal cortex (superior parietal lobule and precuneus) was greater for value-based decisions that took longer, as revealed by psychophysiological interaction (PPI) analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C131-C132 describe PPI analysis results showing RT-dependent connectivity between hippocampus and parietal cortex. The methods are clearly described (C131-C132) and results are presented in Figure 4, providing evidence for a broader network involved in value-based deliberation.

results.result: Control analyses ruled out that hippocampal activation differences were due to object identification demands or RT range differences between tasks. The observation of both a main effect of task and an interaction with RT suggests object recognition does not account for the hippocampal findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 present systematic control analyses addressing alternative explanations. The logic is sound (C30) and supported by data from restricted RT ranges (C32) and the pattern of main effects versus interactions (C31), strengthening the interpretation of hippocampal involvement in deliberation.

results.result: Amnesic patients showed intact performance on perceptual decisions compared to healthy controls, with no significant differences in accuracy, reaction time, or efficiency index. This intact performance is consistent with the hypothesis that perceptual decisions rely on external sensory evidence that does not require hippocampal processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C14, and C40 present converging evidence from multiple measures (accuracy, RT, efficiency) showing preserved perceptual decision-making in patients. Statistical tests are reported with non-significant p-values (C8: p=0.28, p=0.18, p=0.41; C14: p=0.98), and the interpretation is supported by citations to prior work on sensory processing (C40).

results.result: Amnesic patients' choices on value-based decisions were more stochastic (flatter choice function, p=0.0008) and substantially slower (p=0.0004) than healthy controls, with this slowing specific to value-based versus perceptual decisions (interaction p=0.002). Patients' RTs were less driven by subjective value ratings (p=0.015), though they used the rating scale similarly to controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C12 and C36-C37 present a coherent pattern of patient deficits with appropriate statistical tests and p-values. The specificity to value-based decisions (C11) and the dissociation between rating scale use (C36) and choice behavior (C37) strengthen the interpretation that patients have impaired deliberation rather than impaired valuation.

results.result: The efficiency index (accuracy/RT) for value-based decisions was significantly lower in amnesic patients compared to controls (p=0.0007), indicating that patients' additional deliberation time did not improve decision quality. This pattern is inconsistent with a speed-accuracy tradeoff and suggests inefficient deliberative processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C38-C39, and C41 present a novel efficiency metric that integrates accuracy and RT data. The logic is sound (C38-C39), the statistical comparison is significant (C13), and the interpretation follows logically from the pattern of results (C41). This provides strong evidence for qualitatively different deliberation processes in patients.

results.result: An alternative heuristic model (distinguishing trivial vs. non-trivial decisions) was not supported in healthy controls but showed some consistency with amnesic patient data. While the heuristic model did not outperform the drift diffusion model, it highlights qualitative differences in how patients resolve value-based preferences.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C43 and C128-C130 present exploratory analysis of an alternative model. While the model comparison favors drift diffusion (C130), the qualitative pattern in patients (C129: p=0.29 vs. controls p<0.005) is suggestive but not definitive (C43). This analysis raises interesting possibilities but requires further validation.

results.result: The findings link the timing of value-based decisions about familiar options to the hippocampus, suggesting that the hippocampus contributes to deliberative processes by supporting construction of value from internal evidence and comparison between options, rather than simple retrieval of item-value associations.
results.evaluation: Claims C44, C50, C53, C58, C62, C84, and C86 synthesize the main findings and their interpretation. The conclusions are well-supported by the convergence of fMRI (showing RT-related hippocampal activity) and patient data (showing impaired deliberation with hippocampal damage), though the specific mechanisms remain to be fully elucidated.

results.result: The study's central hypothesis is that the hippocampus plays a key role in deliberation during value-based decisions by contributing to comparison between items and construction of internal evidence. This hypothesis is motivated by prior work on hippocampal roles in prospection, relational encoding, and memory-dependent decisions.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C17 and C20-C25 establish the theoretical framework and predictions. The hypothesis is well-grounded in prior literature (C15-C17) with appropriate citations, and the logical predictions (C23-C25) are clearly stated and testable. The subsequent experimental results support these predictions.

results.result: Value-based decisions are typically assumed to rely on subjective value signals in vmPFC, but even familiar choices involve comparison and may require generation of internal evidence to resolve indecision. Prior work suggests simple object-value associations do not depend on the hippocampus, and it is unclear why simple associative memory would account for longer deliberation times.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C49 and C51-C52 establish the theoretical context and gap in understanding. The statements are well-supported by citations (C45-C47, C51) and the logical reasoning is sound (C48-C49, C52), motivating the need for the current study.

results.result: The findings extend recent work demonstrating hippocampal involvement in memory-dependent decisions to show a causal role for the hippocampus in decisions about familiar options. This contributes to a growing shift in understanding hippocampal function beyond episodic memory to include implicit guidance of actions and decisions.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58, C63, and C88 position the current findings within the broader literature. The connections to prior work are appropriate and well-cited (C56-C57, C63, C88), and the claimed contribution is justified by the combination of fMRI and patient data.

results.result: Patients likely rely on degraded, coarser value signals rather than having complete amnesia for item values, as their choices are not arbitrary. Comparison with vmPFC patients (who show stochasticity but not RT slowing) suggests complementary roles for hippocampus and vmPFC in value-based decisions.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C68 present a nuanced interpretation of patient behavior with appropriate comparisons to other patient populations. The reasoning is logical (C64-C65) and supported by citations to relevant literature (C66-C68), though the proposed complementary roles remain somewhat speculative.

results.result: The long decision times in amnesic patients reflect their attempt to engage hippocampal relational mechanisms and their failure to do so. Longer RTs stem from continued effort to generate evidence, while greater stochasticity stems from ultimately falling back on rudimentary, noisier value representations.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 and C79-C80 propose a specific mechanistic interpretation of patient behavior. While this interpretation is plausible and consistent with the data, it remains speculative (C70, C79-C80 use 'propose' and 'possibly'). Alternative explanations are not fully ruled out, and direct evidence for the proposed mechanism is limited.

results.result: In perceptual decisions, evidence samples are independent and identically distributed from the stimulus. In value-based decisions, the analogy breaks down because the stimulus provides only one sample of objects, and the brain likely generates evidence through constructive thought processes rather than independent samples of ΔValue. Alternative integration mechanisms may be indistinguishable from drift diffusion models.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C78 present a theoretical analysis of evidence sampling differences between task types. The reasoning is logical and well-articulated (C71-C75), acknowledges alternative mechanisms (C76-C77), and recognizes model fitting limitations (C78 with citation). This provides important conceptual context for interpreting the findings.

results.result: A limitation of the study is the inability to identify the specific hippocampal-based process guiding deliberation; the study can only observe manifestations in RT and BOLD activity. The study deliberately avoided biasing participants toward memory-based strategies to test whether memory spontaneously contributes to decisions.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C83 acknowledge important limitations and design choices. The recognition of limitations is appropriate and honest (C81-C82), and the justification for the experimental design (C83) is reasonable, though it also limits mechanistic insights.

results.result: The finding that the hippocampus supports deliberation between similar-value options addresses Buridan's paradox and contributes to a shift from viewing the hippocampus solely as supporting episodic memory to recognizing its broader role in guiding behavior through relational associations.
results.evaluation: Claims C85, C87-C88 discuss the broader theoretical implications. The connection to Buridan's paradox is appropriate (C85 with citations), and the contribution to evolving views of hippocampal function is well-articulated and supported by citations (C88).

results.result: The study employed well-controlled experimental procedures including training to criterion, BDM auction for value elicitation with bid revision, systematic pairing of items varying in ΔValue, and matched perceptual and value-based tasks. Experiment 2 used modified procedures appropriate for the patient population.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C113 provide detailed methodological descriptions. The procedures are clearly documented and appropriate for the research questions. The BDM auction (C96-C98) is a standard method with proper citation, and the modifications for Experiment 2 (C109-C113) are reasonable adaptations for the patient population.

results.result: fMRI data were acquired using standard parameters (3T scanner, TR=2s, 2mm in-plane resolution) and preprocessed using FSL with standard procedures including motion correction, spatial smoothing (5mm FWHM), high-pass filtering (100s cutoff), and boundary-based registration to structural images and MNI space.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C121 document imaging acquisition and preprocessing parameters. The methods are standard and appropriate, with proper citations to software packages (C117, C120-C121). The parameters are clearly specified and would support reproducibility.

results.result: The drift diffusion model was fit to choice and RT data by maximizing joint likelihood, solving the Fokker-Planck equation numerically, using time-varying bounds, and optimizing parameters with the Nelder-Mead method from 100 random starting points to avoid local minima.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C127 describe the drift diffusion modeling approach. The methods are appropriate and clearly documented, with proper citations (C126). The use of multiple starting points (C127) is good practice for avoiding local minima. The time-varying bounds (C123) are theoretically motivated.

results.result: Group-level fMRI analyses used FSL's FLAME1 mixed effects modeling with cluster-based correction for whole-brain analyses (z=2.3 cluster-forming, p<0.05 extent) and voxel-based correction for small volume analyses (p<0.05 voxel-level within ROI masks).
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C135 describe statistical analysis and multiple comparisons correction methods. The approaches are standard and appropriate, with proper citations (C133). The thresholds are clearly specified and would control false positive rates.

results.result: Decisions take more time when options are similar in value, potentially due to evidence accumulation to threshold. Open questions remain about whether hippocampal involvement varies with item properties (e.g., natural vs. packaged foods), though all value-based decisions ultimately depend on transforming perceptual input to internal value estimates.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C19 and C59-C61 establish general principles and identify open questions. The statements about decision time are well-established (C18-C19 with citations), and the identification of open questions is appropriate (C59-C61), though these remain speculative.

results.result: Deliberation may involve evaluation of alternatives and prospection about future hypothetical experiences, processes that prior work suggests are likely to engage the hippocampus.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 extend the proposed mechanism with appropriate citations to prior work. The connection is logical and well-supported by literature, though the specific role of these processes in the current task remains to be directly tested.
